meta.title: The AIHL Project — AI & International Humanitarian Law
meta.description: Independent research on synthetic media and the protection of people in armed conflict. Explore MAESTRO4IHL, our framework for examining risks to prisoners of war.

hero.title: The prisoner is real.
hero.subtitle: The video, the voice, the record may not be.
hero.body: A fabricated image can expose a prisoner to humiliation. A false record can obstruct a search. A cloned voice can conceal abuse. We study what these technologies mean for the people protected by the laws of war.
hero.caption: The AIHL Project is an independent research and evaluation initiative.
hero.focus: Our first study: synthetic media and prisoners of war.

problem.label: The problem
problem.title: Protection depends on information people can trust.
problem.intro: A name on a capture card. A message to a family. A record of where someone is held. These connections help prisoners be found, contacted, and accounted for. Synthetic media can corrupt them.
paragraphs: AI in armed conflict raises questions beyond targeting and weapons. It also changes the conditions of captivity: what families can know, what humanitarian institutions can verify, and what the record will show after a war.

Our research follows three conditions that make this information useful: it reflects what happened, it reaches the people entitled to it, and its source can be established. A failure in any one can affect the others.

conditions.name: Accuracy
conditions.text: The record reflects the person’s actual identity, circumstances, and condition.

conditions.name: Access
conditions.text: Information reaches the prisoner, family, authorities, and humanitarian institutions entitled to receive it.

conditions.name: Origin
conditions.text: A record or message can be traced to a source whose identity and authority can be checked.

problem.lifecycleTitle: One false entry can follow a person for years.
problem.lifecycleIntro: A record made at capture can affect detention, correspondence, return home, and later claims. Select a stage to see the kinds of information involved.
problem.asymmetryTitle: The burden cannot fall on the prisoner.
problem.asymmetry: Prisoners and families often have the least access to the tools and evidence needed to check a fabrication. Detaining authorities, technology providers, and institutions control more of the process. Our framework asks what each can do with the capacity it has.
problem.trust: Even a genuine record can lose its force when fabrication is plausible. Preventing false material and preserving confidence in authentic evidence are related tasks.

framework.label: The framework
framework.title: Follow the system. Find the points of failure.
framework.name: MAESTRO4IHL
framework.intro: MAESTRO4IHL is our adaptation of the MAESTRO threat-modeling framework. It follows synthetic media through seven layers, from the model that produces it to the people and institutions affected.
framework.layersIntro: Each layer asks a different question about the same event. Together they connect a technical failure to its consequences for a person in captivity.
framework.adaptationsTitle: Six changes for this research context.
framework.adaptationsIntro: We use MAESTRO’s structure to examine humanitarian protections, the full period of captivity, and the people who may never interact with the AI system itself.
framework.stepsIntro: The six steps organize a case, identify connected failures, set priorities, and choose safeguards to review over time.
framework.attribution: MAESTRO was developed by Ken Huang. MAESTRO4IHL’s humanitarian applications, scenarios, and recommendations are the AIHL Project’s own.

explorer.label: Worked cases
explorer.title: Three fabrications. Three kinds of harm.
explorer.intro: A video, a document, a voice. Follow each hypothetical case through the same six steps to see where technical safeguards and institutional practices meet.
explorer.note: These cases illustrate possible failures. They are not reports of documented incidents. The severity labels are qualitative judgments made for this analysis, not measured probabilities.
explorer.mappingLabel: The seven layers in this case
explorer.sourceNote: Treaty references guide the research. Their application depends on the conflict, the facts, and the person’s legal status.

responsibility.label: Responsibility
responsibility.title: Put the work where the capacity is.
responsibility.intro: States hold records. Developers shape model behavior. Platforms control distribution. Humanitarian institutions and monitors have different access, expertise, and mandates. Effective safeguards require work across these roles.
responsibility.matrixIntro: The matrix proposes where each actor can make its strongest practical contribution. Select a row to compare the five functions.

functions.name: Documentation
functions.text: Preserve accurate records and evidence of how they were created and handled.

functions.name: Detection
functions.text: Identify suspected fabrications and failures in safeguards.

functions.name: Escalation
functions.text: Bring findings to people and institutions able to act.

functions.name: Interdiction
functions.text: Interrupt harmful distribution or use where the actor has authority and control.

functions.name: Hardening
functions.text: Improve systems and practices so the same failure is less likely to recur.

responsibility.note: These weights are qualitative recommendations about defensive work. They are not measured capability scores or a determination of legal duties. Existing obligations require a separate legal assessment.
responsibility.principle: No defensive burden is assigned to prisoners or their families.
responsibility.principleText: Their ability to identify a fake must not become a condition of their protection.

research.label: Research
research.title: The laws of war belong in AI evaluation.
research.intro: The people protected by international humanitarian law must be part of how AI systems are tested. Our first study examines synthetic media and prisoners of war.
paragraphs: The study examines how fabricated media can damage the records and communications that support POW protections. It focuses on dignity, reliable information, and contact with the outside world under the Third Geneva Convention and relevant customary rules.

MAESTRO4IHL adapts a seven-layer threat model to this setting. Three hypothetical cases show how a failure can travel from a generative model into a family’s understanding, a tracing process, or the public record. Six analytic steps connect those failures to proposed safeguards.

The framework also proposes how defensive work can be shared according to practical capacity. It is a basis for testing and discussion. The scenarios and weights are illustrative; they do not establish how often these harms occur or prove that a proposed safeguard will prevent them.
research.thesisTitle: On the case for a sociotechnical turn in red-teaming AI systems in armed conflict
research.thesisDescription: The research argument behind the project: examine how technical systems and institutional practices affect people protected by the laws of war.
research.reference: MAESTRO4IHL: A threat model for synthetic-media violations of prisoner-of-war protections under international humanitarian law. The AIHL Project, 2026.

about.label: About the project
about.title: A technical question. A human consequence.
about.intro: The AIHL Project brings together research on AI evaluation, security, international law, and the institutions that protect people in conflict.
about.mission: We founded the project to study how synthetic media can harm people protected by international humanitarian law. Our first focus is prisoners of war: the records that identify them, the communications that connect them to others, and the dignity they are owed in captivity. MAESTRO4IHL is the framework we developed for that work.

team.name: Nathan Heath
team.summary: Decision scientist and AI safety researcher. Founder and CEO of Syntony.
paragraphs: Nathan Heath is a decision scientist and AI safety researcher with 14 years of experience in geopolitics and emerging technology. He founded Syntony, where he leads AI evaluation, governance, risk advisory, and software work. Previously, as a Senior Research Scientist at National Security Innovations, he worked on emerging technology risk, AI integration, and security cooperation for U.S. government clients.

He red-teams frontier AI systems for OpenAI and Anthropic and serves as an Expert Advisor to the Cloud Security Alliance. He is a Security Fellow with the Truman National Security Project, a member of MIT AI Alignment, and a contributing researcher with the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative. His research examines system dynamics and frontier AI risk, the protection of testimony archives from synthetic media, and defense industrial cooperation in Europe.

Nathan holds an M.A. in Law and Diplomacy from The Fletcher School at Tufts University. He also studied Politics, Philosophy, and Economics at Oxford, and diplomatic and business strategy at Harvard. His work has been presented at UNIDIR, the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI at UNESCO House, the Cambridge Centre for Geopolitics, the Minderoo Centre for Technology & Democracy, the American University of Paris, the International Institute for Justice, and the UK Ministry of Defence’s Deterrence and Assurance Academic Alliance. It has appeared in War on the Rocks, RAND Europe, World Politics Review, PRISM, and The Washington Post.

He writes A Mind of Their Own on AI consciousness, governance, and safety, and contributes to LessWrong. He leads the North Carolina chapter of the OpenAI Forum and contributes research to the Meta Oversight Board and the EvalEval Coalition.

team.name: Wm. Matthew Kennedy, PhD
team.summary: AI+ Senior Research Fellow at King’s College London. Researcher in AI ethics, safety, and political economy.
paragraphs: Wm. Matthew (Matt) Kennedy is an AI+ Senior Research Fellow at King’s College London and a former Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellow at the Oxford Internet Institute. His research examines AI ethics, safety, and political economy, with particular interests in evaluation and red-teaming, AI and knowledge production, education, epistemic harms, and decolonial AI.

He is affiliated with the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance; the Machine Learning & Society team at Women at the Table; the AI and Education at Oxford University research hub; and the Center for AI and Digital Policy. He regularly contributes to Humane Intelligence events and is an inaugural ORF US-India AI Fellow.

Matt earned his PhD at the University of Sydney, studying the history of colonialism, international law, and scientific governance. He subsequently held research fellowships at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Sussex. In the technology industry, he led a small AI evaluation team, collaborated on research in AI ethics, safety, and governance, and advised U.S. and international public officials on AI policy.
At the Oxford Internet Institute, his project examined how the colonial past can inform decisions about the design, development, use, and governance of AI systems.

audiences.name: Platforms
audiences.text: Review how fabricated prisoner media is identified, distributed, and addressed.

audiences.name: Humanitarian institutions
audiences.text: Bring operational knowledge to questions of records, contact, verification, and response.

audiences.name: Policymakers
audiences.text: Examine how dignity, accurate records, and meaningful contact are addressed in AI governance.
